title: Verifier-Grounded Evaluation of LLM-Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We study whether an LLM single-pass generation pipeline produces semantically correct device configurations at verifier scale for operationally meaningful NetOps intents. We preregistered a paired design (N=120 programmatically generated intent→configuration tasks across three topology classes) comparing a deterministic template baseline to gpt-5-mini single-pass generation, using a deterministic open-source validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and a preregistered paired-binary analysis. Result: both conditions achieved verifier pass rate 120/120 (baseline=1.00, gpt-5-mini=1.00), paired difference 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples), McNemar two-sided p=1.0. We release all artifacts and interpret the null result in light of the synthetic task design, deterministic transformation rules, and validator scope. We discuss threats to validity and directions for operationally broader evaluation.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into low-level device configurations for NetOps. Prior work highlights both practical promise and failure modes: LLMs can reduce manual effort but may introduce semantic errors (misordered operations, ACL/BGP-policy regressions) that a surface-level correctness check overlooks [1,2]. We ask: under a reproducible, verifier-grounded confirmatory protocol, does single-pass LLM generation produce fewer verifier failures than a deterministic template baseline? We preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic (CAND‑2026‑001) to answer this question with deterministic validator checks and a paired design. Our contributions: (1) a preregistered, reproducible benchmark and artifacts for verifier-based semantic evaluation; (2) a confirmatory execution (N=120) comparing a deterministic template baseline to gpt-5-mini single-pass generation against an open deterministic validator; (3) a transparent analysis and discussion of operational implications and validity threats.
sections.related_work: Automated and intent-driven configuration generation has been explored across NetOps and infrastructure domains; recent surveys of LLM-based network management document promise and risks including hallucination and incorrect semantic effects [2]. Tools and frameworks for high-fidelity configuration analysis and verification (e.g., Batfish and successors) motivate verifier-grounded evaluation because data‑plane/control‑plane invariants better capture operational correctness than token-level metrics [3]. Prior LLM-for-configuration work has mainly reported plausibility or per-sample success; we instead evaluate verifier-level semantic correctness under a preregistered confirmatory design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study followed preregistration CAND-2026-001-NetConfig-Semantic-v1 (frozen before execution). Task generation: 120 intent→configuration tasks were programmatically synthesized and unit-tested; tasks span three topology classes (edge, datacenter, multi‑AS) and three vendor-syntax families per the preregistration. Conditions: (A) deterministic template baseline; (B) gpt-5-mini single-pass generation (provider recorded as openai_responses; adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1). Execution: a single canonical seed per task for the confirmatory paired test (exploratory seeds reserved per preregistration). Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed intent-constraint validation producing a binary verifier pass/fail per episode with fine-grained validator traces archived. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline over N=120 tasks. Analysis plan: paired estimator = mean_i(llm_i - baseline_i). Inference: 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and exact McNemar two-sided test (pre-specified). Failure handling and stopping: infrastructure failures trigger preregistered retry policy; pairs with both infrastructure failures would be excluded per preregistration; none occurred. Artifacts: all prompts, model responses, validator traces, analysis code, and hashes are published in the study artifact bundle.
sections.results: Execution and primary confirmatory analysis followed the preregistered pipeline. Completed pairs: 120/120. Outcomes: baseline_successes = 120/120 (1.00), gpt-5-mini_successes = 120/120 (1.00). Paired contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00. Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 replicates) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. No infrastructure or scoring failures occurred; contamination detection (string-overlap heuristics) returned no suspected contamination flags for the confirmatory items. Representative task and validator traces are archived (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json). The preregistered exploratory analyses (seed sensitivity, rank stability, and semantic-error taxonomy) were also prepared; because the confirmatory outcome contained no verifier failures, exploratory diagnostics showed no discordant seeds in the confirmatory seed_0 runs and no error classes to summarize.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: under the controlled, synthetic task set, deterministic transformation rules, and the chosen open deterministic validator, gpt-5-mini matched the deterministic template baseline on all confirmatory tasks. This null difference does not imply general equivalence in broader operational settings. Key reasons: (1) synthetic tasks were generated from templates whose solution forms were regular and fully specified by the transformation rules used to create the baseline reference; (2) the validator enforces the pre-specified semantic constraints used to synthesize tasks, so tasks favor syntactic/semantic regularity; (3) using a single canonical seed for confirmatory assessment reduces observed model variability by design. Operational implications: verifier-grounded evaluation is necessary to surface semantic correctness; however, benchmarks must include open, heterogenous, and adversarial task distributions and multiple model seeds to probe realistic failure modes. Recommendations: expand to (i) larger, less templated task banks, (ii) multi-seed sampling, (iii) additional validators/emulators that exercise dynamic control-plane interactions (BGP policy interactions, ACL reachability under failures), and (iv) human‑operational studies comparing guarded agentic pipelines under real observability constraints.
sections.conclusion: We present a preregistered, verifier-grounded short study comparing deterministic templates and an LLM single-pass generator on 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks. Result: both achieved perfect verifier pass rates in this controlled setting (paired difference 0.00, 95% CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p=1.0). The outcome highlights two points: verifier-based metrics enable precise, operationally meaningful measurement; and null results on synthetically regular tasks do not imply safety or generality in production. We release the full artifact bundle to support broader, more adversarial evaluations and invite follow-up studies that vary task realism, model seeds, validator scope, and deployment assumptions to better characterize LLM operational reliability for NetOps automation.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: tasks were programmatically synthesized from deterministic templates and transformation rules; this favors regular solution forms and limits generality to realistic, heterogeneous operational intents.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary design used one canonical seed per task; model variability under multiple independent seeds was reserved for exploratory analysis and is not reflected in the confirmatory result.

Validator scope: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 verifies the preregistered semantic constraints used to synthesize tasks; it may not capture dynamic control-plane interactions or real-world vendor implementation idiosyncrasies.

Possible training-data exposure: exact-proof of model exposure to task templates/training data cannot be excluded by string-overlap heuristics alone; preregistered contamination sensitivity analyses are provided but residual uncertainty remains.
Single-model result: findings apply to gpt-5-mini under the recorded execution conditions and do not generalize across LLM families or agentic multi-step pipelines.
